title: I Was Marking Assessments From My Son's Hospital Room
author: Trudy
summary: Writing at Brolga Education, teacher Trudy reflects on a formative memory: marking student assessments in her lap while sitting beside her son during a hospital stay for seizures, work no one at school had asked her to do but that she felt compelled to complete anyway. She traces this compulsion to the specific skill set teaching builds -- functioning regardless of what is happening around you -- and to years spent simultaneously parenting a profoundly deaf son with complex additional needs while continuing to teach, work she once called resilience but now recognizes as a habit of putting herself last. Her turning point was realizing that waiting for life to "become less busy" before addressing her own wellbeing was a trap, since life never actually became less full; she has since replaced that wait-and-overhaul mindset with small, consistent self-care habits. The piece's sharpest observation about the teaching profession is that wellbeing advice itself can become one more item on an already overloaded improvement checklist, and that teachers who are already carrying a great deal don't need another area of life in which to feel they aren't doing enough.
points: Trudy identifies teaching's core occupational skill -- functioning regardless of what is happening around you -- as the same trait that led her to mark student assessments from her son's hospital bedside despite no pressure from school to do so.

Her key realization is that waiting for life to "become less busy" before prioritizing her own wellbeing was a trap, since across years of teaching, parenting a son with complex needs, and eventually homeschooling him, life never actually became less full.

She argues that standard wellbeing advice (drink more water, meditate, establish boundaries) can itself become another item on an already overloaded improvement checklist for teachers, adding a new area to feel inadequate in rather than relieving existing load.
Her practical shift was from seeking a dramatic overhaul of her habits toward small, consistent choices, on the grounds that consistency proved far more sustainable for her than intensity.
quotes: I have a very clear memory of sitting beside my son in hospital with assessment papers in my lap, marking student assessments while he was being treated for seizures. Nobody from school had asked me to do that.
There are parts of that resilience that I am still incredibly proud of, but I can also see now that I had become very comfortable with putting myself last.
For years, I approached looking after myself as something I would get to when I had more capacity. The problem was that life kept changing, but it never really became less full.

Then wellbeing enters the conversation and somehow that can become another list too: Drink more water. Exercise regularly. Meditate. Meal prep. Establish boundaries. Sleep eight hours. Make time for yourself.
When you are already carrying a lot, you probably don't need another area of your life in which you feel as though you aren't doing enough. I certainly didn't.
I don't think I needed to become better at carrying everything. I think I needed to realise that I was one of the people worth looking after too.
